content: If pus is draining from the ear, instruct the mother on how to dry the ear using a wicking technique. Advise her to perform this procedure three times daily until the pus is no longer present. Additionally, caution her against placing any objects in the ear between wicking treatments. The child should also avoid swimming or getting water in the ear. If the child has a fever causing discomfort, administer paracetamol. For ear infections, if the discharge or pain persists after five days, continue the same antibiotic treatment and wicking for an additional five days. If pus has been draining for two or more weeks, the child likely has chronic otitis media. This diagnosis is based on a history of prolonged ear discharge and can be confirmed through otoscopy. Treat the child as an outpatient by keeping the ear dry through wicking and instilling topical antibiotic drops containing quinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, or ofloxacin) twice daily for two weeks. Quinolone-based drops are more effective than other antibiotics, and antiseptics are not recommended for treating chronic otitis media in children. If necessary, administer parenteral antibiotics effective against Pseudomonas (e.g., gentamicin, azlocillin, or ceftazidime) or initiate tuberculosis treatment after confirmation. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are common in young boys due to posterior urethral valves and in older female infants and children. When bacterial culture is unavailable, diagnosis relies on clinical signs and microscopy of a good-quality urine sample. Symptoms in young children may include fever lasting 24 hours or more without an obvious cause, vomiting, poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, failure to thrive, abdominal pain, or jaundice in neonates. Older children may experience increased frequency, painful urination, or loin pain. Half of infants with UTIs present with fever as the sole symptom, making urine testing essential. Examine a clean, fresh urine sample under a microscope; more than five white cells per high-power field or a positive dipstick test for leukocytes suggests infection. If microscopy and dipstick tests are negative, rule out UTI. Treat UTIs with oral antibiotics for 7–10 days unless there are signs of systemic upset, pyelonephritis, or the child is an infant. Suitable antibiotics include co-trimoxazole, ampicillin, amoxicillin, or cephalexin, depending on local bacterial sensitivity patterns. Encourage fluid intake to prevent dehydration and assist in clearing the infection. Follow up on recurrent UTIs to identify potential anatomical causes, which may require referral for ultrasound investigations. Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis, often caused by bacterial spread through the bloodstream, presents with fever, refusal to move the affected limb, and localized swelling or tenderness. Septic arthritis typically involves a hot, swollen, tender joint with reduced movement. Chronic cases may suggest tuberculosis, especially with discharging sinuses or other TB signs. Early X-rays are not diagnostic, but joint aspiration can confirm infection. Common pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus in children over three years and Haemophilus influenzae type b, Streptococcus pneumoniae, or S. pyogenes in younger children. Treat with appropriate antibiotics based on culture results or empirically with cloxacillin or flucloxacillin. For septic arthritis, remove pus via aspiration or surgical drainage if necessary. Continue antibiotics for three weeks for septic arthritis and five weeks for osteomyelitis. In cases of tuberculosis osteomyelitis, follow national TB treatment guidelines. Dengue fever, caused by an arbovirus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, often begins with acute fever, retro-orbital pain, and high temperatures lasting 2–7 days. Severe cases may involve plasma leakage, shock, or bleeding. Suspect dengue in children with fever lasting more than two days in endemic areas. Symptoms may include headache, joint pain, abdominal pain, vomiting, or rash. Most children recover with supportive care, including oral fluids and paracetamol for fever. Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs due to bleeding risks. Monitor for severe disease signs, such as mucosal bleeding, shock, or rapid hematocrit rise. Admit children with severe dengue for IV fluid management and close monitoring. Use isotonic solutions like normal saline or Ringer’s lactate, adjusting fluid rates based on clinical response. Treat hemorrhagic complications with blood transfusions if necessary, and manage fluid overload cautiously to prevent pulmonary edema or cardiac failure. Rheumatic fever, a complication of Streptococcus pyogenes infection, can cause fever, migratory joint pain, and heart valve damage, leading to respiratory distress or heart failure. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria, including major manifestations like carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, or subcutaneous nodules, and evidence of prior streptococcal infection. Treat with aspirin for joint pain and corticosteroids for severe carditis. Eradicate streptococcal infection with antibiotics and provide long-term prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin to prevent recurrence. Severe acute malnutrition is defined by bilateral pitting edema or severe wasting (weight-for-height < -3 SD or mid-upper arm circumference < 115 mm). Children with appetite loss or medical complications require inpatient care, while those with good appetite and no complications can be managed as outpatients. Conduct a full clinical examination to identify danger signs, infections, or vitamin deficiencies. Treat complications and provide therapeutic feeding.
